messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aisha Khan was a 23-year-old South Asian woman who came to treatment several months after a terrible mistake at work had left another person seriously injured. She described the event as happening during a routine afternoon at her UX design job, when she was moving quickly between meetings and trying to finish a presentation under pressure. In the confusion of the day, her actions contributed to an accident that injured a client she had been coordinating with, and what stayed with her most was not only the immediate shock but the sight of the person on the ground and the helplessness of not being able to undo what had happened. Since then, Aisha had found that anything at her workplace could pull her back into that moment: the same conference room, the layout of her desk, the buzz of a packed office, even an email thread about a project she had touched. Seeing someone who looked like the injured client could make her stomach drop, and any reminder of victims in news stories or in passing conversations would bring up the same hard image of the person she hurt.

In the weeks that followed, Aisha began to live as though she could keep the memory at bay by trying to control it. She would dwell for hours on how the event could have been prevented, replaying every decision and telling herself that if she had been more careful, slower, or less distracted, nobody would have been hurt. At the same time, she tried hard not to think about the trauma at all, forcing herself to push the images away whenever they surfaced. But the more she fought them, the more readily they seemed to intrude, especially once she was back in the environment where it happened. At work, even ordinary tasks started to feel loaded with danger because the office itself had become a reminder, and being surrounded by the same desks, screens, and meeting spaces made the event feel close enough to happen again. The reminders of the victim and the similarity of certain faces only intensified the pressure, and each trigger seemed to send her back into the same exhausting effort to suppress the memory or mentally reconstruct the accident in hopes of finding the moment she should have stopped it.

That effort had spread into her daily life outside the office as well. Aisha stopped driving and refused to ride as a passenger in a vehicle, saying she could not bear the sense of being trapped in a moving space with no easy way to escape her thoughts. Her husband had started handling most errands and long drives, and although he tried to be patient, she noticed the change in how dependent she had become on him. The avoidance brought brief relief, but it also narrowed her world, and the more she arranged her days around not seeing the right places, people, or situations, the more the workplace and the memory of the injured person stood out in her mind as threats she could not safely face. She would catch sight of someone in a lobby or on the street who resembled the victim and feel a wave of panic that sent her back into rumination, asking herself again what she might have done differently, then trying harder not to think at all. Even after she left the office, she could not really leave the event behind; the effort to shut it out only seemed to make the reminders sharper when they appeared.

By the time she sought help, Aisha was exhausted by how tightly her life had shrunk around these efforts. She had been pushing through at work but felt increasingly on edge in the very setting where she needed to function, and she was worried that her fear of reminders, her constant self-reproach, and her refusal to drive were beginning to take over both her marriage and her career. What finally brought her in was the sense that she could no longer keep managing the accident by thinking about it endlessly and then trying to suppress it, because both strategies seemed to keep her stuck. She said she was most afraid that if she let herself think about what happened, she would be overwhelmed by guilt and never recover, yet she was also hoping that therapy might help her stop living as though every workplace conversation, every face, and every car ride might return her to that single moment.
